title: Pretending to be Handicapped

full_text:
A severe festival season brought crowds of wealthy pilgrims to the regional temple town, and professional alms-seekers were collecting silver and gold by displaying various infirmities: the lame were given bags of rice; the blind received copper coins, and the mute were gifted sweet rice puddings.

Observing this flourishing economy from a tea stall, Asadan whispered to Peedan: 'Look at the fortune those beggars are collecting! Our ashram treasury is empty; why should we labor in the garden when a simple display of infirmity can fill our pockets?'

Peedan hesitated: 'But brother, the revered Guru teaches that we must always be truthful!'

Asadan scoffed: 'This is not deceit; this is the philosophical enactment of suffering! I will pretend to be completely blind, and you will pretend to be deaf and mute! We will collect silver, purchase sweet jalebis, and present them to our Master!'

Peedan agreed, captivated by the thought of jalebis.

Asadan tied a dirty cloth tightly over his eyes, took a crooked stick, and began tapping the flagstones, crying in a mournful, nasal whine: 'Charity, noble pilgrims! Pity a poor, blind wanderer who has never seen the light of the sun!'

Beside him sat Peedan, rocking back and forth, pointing to his open mouth and making strange guttural noises: 'Aaah-ooh! Aaah-ooh!'

Charitable pilgrims tossed copper coins into their brass bowl. Within an hour, they had collected nearly two rupees.

Presently, a wealthy village landlord who was known for his sharp skepticism and short temper walked past. Hearing Asadan's wailing, the landlord paused, observing the two 'beggars' closely.

The landlord drew a shining silver rupee from his purse and held it out, saying softly: 'I have a whole silver rupee for the blind man, if he can tell me where my hand is!'

Asadan, eager for the silver rupee, peeked from beneath the loose edge of his blindfold, reached out his hand with perfect precision, and snatched the coin right from the landlord's palm!

'Aha!' shouted the landlord, his eyes blazing with fury. 'A blind man who spots a coin from three paces away! You are an imposter and a thief!'

The landlord raised his heavy walking staff to strike Asadan.

Seeing the stick descending, the 'deaf and mute' Peedan sprang to his feet, leaped two yards into the air, and shouted at the top of his lungs in crystal-clear speech: 'Run, Asadan, run! The landlord is going to beat your brains out!'

Hearing the deaf-mute shout with the voice of a temple bell, the gathered crowd of pilgrims gasped, then erupted in furious indignation: 'Swindlers! Rogues! They have mocked our charity!'

The angry crowd chased the two terrified disciples through the bazaar, pelting them with rotten papayas, mango skins, and old sandals. Bruised, battered, and covered in fruit pulp, Asadan and Peedan sprinted all the way back to the ashram and collapsed at Guru Paramartha's feet.

Hearing their breathless confession, the Guru stroked his beard and delivered a profound lecture: 'You failed, my children, because your philosophical enactment was incomplete! If you choose to be blind, you must blind yourself thoroughly; and if you choose to be mute, you must cut out your tongue! Half-measures in philosophy always end in rotten papayas!'

Rubbing their bruised ribs, the disciples vowed never to enter the profession of mendicancy again.
moral: Pretending infirmity to gain unearned charity brings real humiliation and pain.

quiz.question: What is the central moral lesson taught in "Pretending to be Handicapped"?
options: Foolishness of book knowledge without worldly wisdom
Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof
quiz.hint: Remember the moral lesson of this traditional story.

quiz.question: How do the characters overcome their challenge?
options: Through patience, calm reflection, and wisdom
By shouting loudly and blaming others
By running away from every problem
quiz.hint: Consider the virtues praised in world folklore.

quiz.question: What memorable conclusion does this story teach young readers?
options: Honesty, kindness, and clear thinking lead to peace

the ability to judge well and understand the truth
